subtopics.name: Classes & Objects
subtopics.content: Classes are blueprints or templates that define the structure and behavior of objects in Java. An object is an instance of a class that holds actual values and can invoke methods. A class contains fields (variables) to store data and methods to define behavior. Understanding how to define classes, create objects, and access members using the dot operator is the foundation of object-oriented programming in Java.

videos.title: Classes & Objects
videos.ai_context: Video tutorial covering Classes & Objects in Object Oriented Programming in Java.

subtopics.name: Constructors
subtopics.content: Constructors are special methods in Java used to initialize objects when they are created. They have the same name as the class and no return type. Java supports default constructors, parameterized constructors, and copy constructors. Constructor overloading allows creating multiple constructors with different parameter lists. Understanding constructors is essential for proper object initialization and managing object state.

videos.title: Constructors
videos.ai_context: Video tutorial covering Constructors in Object Oriented Programming in Java.

subtopics.name: this, static & final Keyword
subtopics.content: The 'this' keyword refers to the current object instance and is used to distinguish between instance variables and parameters, invoke other constructors, and pass the current object as an argument. The 'static' keyword indicates that a member belongs to the class rather than any specific instance — static variables are shared across all objects and static methods can be called without creating an object. The 'final' keyword restricts modification: a final variable becomes a constant, a final method cannot be overridden, and a final class cannot be extended.

videos.title: this, static & final Keyword
videos.ai_context: Video tutorial covering this, static & final Keyword in Object Oriented Programming in Java.

subtopics.name: Inheritance
subtopics.content: Inheritance is an OOP mechanism where a child class (subclass) acquires the properties and behaviors of a parent class (superclass) using the 'extends' keyword. It promotes code reusability and establishes an IS-A relationship between classes. Java supports single and multilevel inheritance but does not support multiple inheritance with classes. The 'super' keyword is used to access parent class members and constructors.

videos.title: Inheritance
videos.ai_context: Video tutorial covering Inheritance in Object Oriented Programming in Java.

subtopics.name: Polymorphism
subtopics.content: Polymorphism means 'many forms' and allows objects to be treated as instances of their parent class. Java supports two types: compile-time polymorphism (method overloading) and runtime polymorphism (method overriding). Runtime polymorphism is achieved through dynamic method dispatch, where the JVM determines which method to invoke at runtime based on the actual object type. Polymorphism enables flexible and extensible code design.

videos.title: Polymorphism
videos.ai_context: Video tutorial covering Polymorphism in Object Oriented Programming in Java.

subtopics.name: Abstraction & Encapsulation
subtopics.content: Abstraction is the process of hiding implementation details and exposing only essential features, achieved through abstract classes and interfaces. Encapsulation is the practice of bundling data and methods within a single class while restricting direct access to internal state using private variables and public getter/setter methods. Together, abstraction and encapsulation form the core principles of object-oriented design, promoting data integrity, reduced coupling, and maintainable code.

videos.title: Abstraction & Encapsulation
videos.ai_context: Video tutorial covering Abstraction & Encapsulation in Object Oriented Programming in Java.

subtopics.name: Interfaces
subtopics.content: An interface in Java is a reference type that defines a contract of abstract methods that implementing classes must fulfill. Interfaces support multiple inheritance in Java, as a class can implement multiple interfaces. From Java 8 onwards, interfaces can also contain default methods and static methods. Interfaces are fundamental for achieving loose coupling, abstraction, and designing plug-and-play architectures.

videos.title: Interfaces
videos.ai_context: Video tutorial covering Interfaces in Object Oriented Programming in Java.

subtopics.name: Method Overloading & Overriding
subtopics.content: Method overloading is a compile-time polymorphism feature that allows multiple methods with the same name but different parameter lists within a class. Method overriding is a runtime polymorphism feature where a subclass provides a specific implementation of a method already defined in its superclass, using the @Override annotation. Overloading is resolved by the compiler based on arguments, while overriding is resolved by the JVM at runtime based on the actual object type. Both techniques are essential for flexible and extensible Java applications.

videos.title: Method Overloading & Overriding
videos.ai_context: Video tutorial covering Method Overloading & Overriding in Object Oriented Programming in Java.

subtopics.name: Object Class
subtopics.content: The Object class is the root class of the Java class hierarchy. Every class in Java implicitly extends the Object class, inheriting its methods such as toString(), equals(), hashCode(), clone(), getClass(), finalize(), wait(), notify(), and notifyAll(). Understanding the Object class is important because its methods are available to all Java objects and are often overridden to provide meaningful behavior specific to each class.

videos.title: Object Class
videos.ai_context: Video tutorial covering Object Class in Object Oriented Programming in Java.

subtopics.name: equals() & hashCode()
subtopics.content: The equals() method is used to compare two objects for logical equality, while hashCode() returns an integer hash code value for an object. By default, equals() checks reference equality and hashCode() returns a memory-based value. When overriding equals(), hashCode() must also be overridden to maintain the contract: equal objects must have the same hash code. These methods are critical for correct behavior in hash-based collections like HashMap and HashSet.

For input '2 John 3 Alex', the expected output is 'false'.

solutions.title: robust equals

hints: Always override hashCode when overriding equals
